### Problem: Mirror grid {#sec-mat-p2-mirror}

::: {.p-statement}
You are given an $n \times n$ grid of `0`s and `1`s. One operation flips one cell. Find the minimum number of operations after which the grid looks the same when rotated by $0^\circ$, $90^\circ$, $180^\circ$ and $270^\circ$.

$1 \le t \le 100$ test cases, $1 \le n \le 100$. The grid `010 / 110 / 010` needs $1$ flip; the $1 \times 1$ grid `0` needs $0$.

Source: [CF 1703E · Mirror Grid](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1703/E){.solved rating="1200"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
A $90^\circ$ rotation moves every cell around an orbit of at most four cells, $(i,j) \to (j,n-1-i) \to (n-1-i,n-1-j) \to (n-1-j,i)$, so a grid that survives every rotation is one where each orbit is all `0` or all `1`. Orbits never share a cell, so each one is fixed on its own: an orbit of four cells holding $k$ ones costs $\min(k, 4-k)$ flips.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Rotate and compare.** Build the three rotated grids with the formula of @sec-mat-a3 and read, for every cell, the four values that land on it. That is the cell's orbit, but each four-cell orbit is met once from each of its four members, so the sum of the costs is four times too big. $O(n^2)$ time and $O(n^2)$ extra memory for the copies.
2. **Walk each orbit once.** Never build a rotated grid. Use the four-cycle of @sec-mat-p2-rotate as a list of coordinates: for $i < \lceil n/2 \rceil$ and $j < \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ the cell $(i,j)$ is the representative of exactly one four-cell orbit, and for odd $n$ the centre is a one-cell orbit that costs nothing. Count the ones $k$ in the orbit and add $\min(k, 4-k)$. $O(n^2)$ time, $O(1)$ extra memory.

**Invariant.** The orbits partition the grid (@sec-mat-a6), and a grid is unchanged by the $90^\circ$ rotation exactly when it is constant on every orbit. So the costs of different orbits add up, and the cheapest fix of one orbit is to copy its majority value onto the minority.
:::

::: {#fig-mat-p2-mirror}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def _mirror_orbits(n):
    reps = [(i, j) for i in range((n + 1) // 2) for j in range(n // 2)]
    lab = {}
    for k, (i, j) in enumerate(reps):
        for a, b in [(i, j), (j, n - 1 - i), (n - 1 - i, n - 1 - j), (n - 1 - j, i)]:
            lab[(a, b)] = k
    return reps, lab


mg_grid = ["11100", "11011", "01011", "10011", "11000"]
mg_reps, mg_lab = _mirror_orbits(5)
assert len(mg_reps) == 6 and len(mg_lab) == 24          # six four-cell orbits + the centre
mg_pal = ["indigo", "cyan", "green", "amber", "pink", "violet"]


def draw(ax, p):
    cols = {cell: mg_pal[k] for cell, k in mg_lab.items()}
    V.grid(ax, p, [list(r) for r in mg_grid], colors=cols, cell_w=0.9)
    V.text(ax, p, 2.25, -4.8, "same colour = one orbit of the 90-degree rotation; the centre is alone",
           size=9, color="muted")
V.show(draw)
```

A $5 \times 5$ grid (the third sample) with its six four-cell orbits coloured. Each colour appears once in each quarter of the grid. The answer adds $\min(k, 4-k)$ over the colours, and the uncoloured centre is free.

:::

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Rotate and compare

::: {.form-next}
Build the three rotated grids with `rot[j][n-1-i] = g[i][j]`. Cell $(i,j)$ then sees its whole orbit as the four values at $(i,j)$ in the four grids. Summing $\min(k, 4-k)$ over all $n^2$ cells counts every four-cell orbit four times, so divide by four; the centre of an odd grid adds $0$ because its four values are equal. $O(n^2)$ time, $O(n^2)$ extra memory.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def mirror_brute(g):
    n = len(g)
    grids = [[[int(ch) for ch in row] for row in g]]
    for _ in range(3):
        a = grids[-1]
        rot = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
        for i in range(n):
            for j in range(n):
                rot[j][n - 1 - i] = a[i][j]
        grids.append(rot)
    total = 0
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(n):
            k = sum(G[i][j] for G in grids)
            total += min(k, 4 - k)
    return total // 4


assert mirror_brute(["010", "110", "010"]) == 1
assert mirror_brute(["0"]) == 0
```

##### C++

```cpp
int mirrorBrute(const vector<string>& g) {
    int n = g.size();
    vector<vector<vector<int>>> G(4, vector<vector<int>>(n, vector<int>(n)));
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        for (int j = 0; j < n; ++j) G[0][i][j] = g[i][j] - '0';
    for (int r = 1; r < 4; ++r)
        for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
            for (int j = 0; j < n; ++j) G[r][j][n - 1 - i] = G[r - 1][i][j];
    int total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        for (int j = 0; j < n; ++j) {
            int k = G[0][i][j] + G[1][i][j] + G[2][i][j] + G[3][i][j];
            total += min(k, 4 - k);
        }
    return total / 4;
}
```
:::

#### Walk each orbit once

::: {.form-next}
Visit only the representatives $(i,j)$ with $i < \lceil n/2 \rceil$ and $j < \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$. Each one reads its four cells straight from the input with the four-cycle coordinates, so nothing is copied and nothing is counted twice. $O(n^2)$ time, $O(1)$ extra memory.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def mirror_grid(g):
    n = len(g)
    total = 0
    for i in range((n + 1) // 2):
        for j in range(n // 2):
            k = (int(g[i][j]) + int(g[j][n - 1 - i])
                 + int(g[n - 1 - i][n - 1 - j]) + int(g[n - 1 - j][i]))
            total += min(k, 4 - k)
    return total


mg_samples = [(["010", "110", "010"], 1), (["0"], 0),
              (["11100", "11011", "01011", "10011", "11000"], 9),
              (["01000", "10101", "01010", "00010", "01001"], 7),
              (["11001", "00000", "11111", "10110", "01111"], 6)]
for mg_g, mg_want in mg_samples:
    assert mirror_grid(mg_g) == mirror_brute(mg_g) == mg_want
for _ in range(300):
    n = random.randint(1, 7)
    g = ["".join(random.choice("01") for _ in range(n)) for _ in range(n)]
    assert mirror_grid(g) == mirror_brute(g)
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    int t;
    if (!(cin >> t)) return 0;
    while (t--) {
        int n;
        cin >> n;
        vector<string> g(n);
        for (auto& row : g) cin >> row;
        int total = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < (n + 1) / 2; ++i)
            for (int j = 0; j < n / 2; ++j) {
                int k = (g[i][j] - '0') + (g[j][n - 1 - i] - '0')
                      + (g[n - 1 - i][n - 1 - j] - '0') + (g[n - 1 - j][i] - '0');
                total += min(k, 4 - k);
            }
        cout << total << "\n";
    }
}
```
:::
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Rotate and compare**: $O(n^2)$ time, $O(n^2)$ extra memory for the three rotated copies. **Walk each orbit once**: $O(n^2)$ time (every cell is read once), $O(1)$ extra memory. Both are far inside the limits; the second form wins because there is less to get wrong, not because it is asymptotically faster.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- $n = 1$: there are no four-cell orbits (`n // 2 == 0`), and the answer is $0$.
- Odd $n$: the representatives fill a $\lceil n/2 \rceil \times \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ block, which is $(n^2-1)/4$ orbits; the centre is left out because it never moves.
- Even $n$: the block is $\frac n2 \times \frac n2$, which is $n^2/4$ orbits, and there is no centre.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- **Looping over a square $\lceil n/2 \rceil \times \lceil n/2 \rceil$ block.** For odd $n$ that visits some orbits twice (from two different members) and over-counts.
- **Fixing cells pair by pair.** Making a cell agree with one orbit-mate and then checking the next pair is not optimal; decide the whole orbit by majority at once.
:::

**Variants.** [CF 1422B · Nice Matrix](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1422/B){rating="1300"} uses the orbits of *two reflections* — cells $(i,j)$, $(i,m-1-j)$, $(n-1-i,j)$, $(n-1-i,m-1-j)$ — and a change costs the distance a value moves, so each orbit is set to its median instead of its majority. [LC 1886 · Determine Whether Matrix Can Be Obtained By Rotation](https://leetcode.com/problems/determine-whether-matrix-can-be-obtained-by-rotation/){difficulty="Easy"} asks the opposite question: given two grids, is one a rotation of the other? Check the four index formulas of @sec-mat-a3 without building any rotated copy.
